strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and somewhat counter-intuitive perspective connecting component-level smoothness/Lipschitz properties ('plasticity') to finetuning performance, explicitly contrasting with the common assumption that smoothness aids adaptation.

Solid theoretical contribution: derives rigorous upper bounds on the plasticity of LayerNorm, feedforward layers, and multi-head self-attention (including a tighter bound using an image-energy argument), with full proofs provided in the appendix.

Very extensive empirical validation: plasticity measured across 11 diverse classification benchmarks, three ViT scales (86M/307M/632M), and extended to DINOv3 and GPT-2, consistently confirming the theoretical ranking MHA > FC1 > FC2 > LN2 > LN1.

Large-scale finetuning study (~1000 runs) with both SGD and Adam, multiple learning rates and seeds, plus a low-data VTAB-style regime, showing a consistent and statistically tested (Wilcoxon) relationship between plasticity and finetuning accuracy/stability.
Good mechanistic story linking plasticity to gradient norm magnitude and loss descent speed during optimization (Fig. 1, 5), which is empirically verified rather than just asserted.
Strong attention to reproducibility: released code, detailed hyperparameters/preprocessing, and carbon footprint reporting.
Interesting practical byproducts, e.g., single-component (LayerNorm) finetuning with Adam outperforming LoRA with far fewer parameters, showing parameter count alone doesn't determine adaptability.
weaknesses: The theoretical upper bounds are extremely loose for the attention module (orders of magnitude larger than empirically observed plasticity, acknowledged in Appendix E.1.1), so the theoretical 'ranking' argument is essentially qualitative/heuristic rather than a tight, predictive quantitative result; the actual ordering is established mainly by direct empirical measurement.

The finetuning experiments only tune one component type at a time (isolated), which is a somewhat artificial setting relative to how PEFT is typically used in practice (combining multiple module types, e.g., attention + norms, or LoRA across several projections); it is unclear how well the 'prioritize high-plasticity components' recommendation generalizes to joint/combined tuning scenarios.

Confounding between plasticity and parameter count is not fully disentangled: MHA/FFN have ~28M trainable parameters vs. ~18K for LayerNorms, so higher capacity alone could partly explain better finetuning performance; while the paper offers one LoRA comparison to argue against a pure parameter-count explanation, a more direct controlled ablation (e.g., comparably-sized non-smooth vs. smooth modules) would strengthen the causal claim.

Reported accuracy gains from prioritizing MHA over LayerNorms are numerically modest in many settings (roughly 1 accuracy point on average across 11 benchmarks), so while statistically significant, the practical significance for real deployment decisions is not fully established.

The finding that attention benefits most from finetuning partially overlaps with prior empirical results (e.g., Touvron et al. 2022), somewhat tempering the novelty of the practical takeaway, even though the theoretical framing (plasticity) is new.

The plasticity metric itself (average rate of change over pretraining vs. downstream image pairs) is a proxy quantity whose direct causal link to finetuning benefit (beyond correlating with gradient norms, which is separately and more directly shown) could be discussed more critically.

strengths: The paper provides a coherent theoretical framework (Definition 1, Propositions 1-4) linking module 'plasticity' (average Lipschitz-type rate of change) to finetuning behavior, with full proofs in the appendix.

Extensive empirical validation: plasticity is measured across 11 benchmarks, two model scales (ViT-Base 86M, ViT-Huge 632M), and the empirical ranking (MHA > FC1 > FC2 > LN2 > LN1) is highly consistent with theory across nearly all settings shown in the extensive appendix figures.
The finetuning study is large-scale and careful (~800 runs, multiple learning rates, 3 seeds per configuration), and robustness/statistical testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank) is reported.

The connection drawn between input-output Lipschitz continuity and gradient norms during optimization is a clear, testable mechanistic story, and the gradient-norm/validation-loss trends in the appendix consistently support the narrative.
The related work and limitations sections are thorough and honest, and the paper is clearly written with good figures summarizing the pipeline (Fig. 2).
weaknesses: Significant confound: MHA/FC1/FC2 each have ~28M trainable parameters while LN1/LN2 have only ~18K (Table 3). The reported performance gap could largely be attributable to trainable capacity rather than 'plasticity' per se; the paper does not control for parameter count (e.g., comparing plastic vs equally-sized less-plastic subsets, or normalizing by parameter count) to isolate the causal effect claimed.

The practical effect sizes are small: full-finetuning baseline (90.9%) is on par with or only marginally better than MHA-only tuning (90.8%), and the decrease between MHA and FC1 is only 0.07% (not statistically significant per Table 1), undermining the strength of the 'components to prioritize' recommendation beyond what is already known (MHA/FFN > LayerNorm), which is consistent with prior empirical findings (e.g., Touvron et al. 2022; Ye et al. 2023) that this paper mainly re-confirms rather than substantially extends.

The theoretical upper bounds (Proposition 3/4) are acknowledged to be extremely loose (orders of magnitude, ~10^6) relative to observed plasticity values, so the 'theory' mainly provides a qualitative ranking rather than quantitatively predictive bounds; the paper leans on this qualitative ranking as its central theoretical contribution.

No new adaptation method is proposed; the paper is purely observational/analytical, with the combination with reparameterization methods (e.g., LoRA on plastic components) left as future work, limiting immediate practical impact.

Some theoretical assumptions (e.g., identical per-position mean/std across tokens for the LayerNorm bound, bounded-energy image assumption) are somewhat strong and not empirically verified, though the paper argues informally for their plausibility.

The component-wise 'in isolation' study, while methodologically clean, does not test realistic combinations (e.g., MHA+FFN jointly vs. LayerNorm-only), which is closer to how PEFT methods are used in practice, limiting the direct actionability of the guidance.
